nodes.label: Alexander at the Indus
nodes.full: Nearchus, sailing from the Indus to the Euphrates with Alexander’s fleet, reports an Indian reed that gives honey without bees — the first Greek contact with cane juice, preserved in Strabo 15.1.20. That report belongs to the Ancient sugar folio; it is the external cause of the whole Greek and Roman reed-honey tradition.
nodes.src: added on review — not an entry of this folio; Strabo 15.1.20 (Radt) via Bouras-Vallianatos (2021) n.20; Ouerfelli (2008) p.18

nodes.label: Theophrastus
nodes.full: Theophrastus says honey comes from flowers, from the air and from reeds. Whether the reed honey is Indian cane or bamboo manna is unclear.

nodes.label: Monsoon route
nodes.full: Greek and Roman captains learn to ride the south-west monsoon straight across the Indian Ocean, making the Egypt–India voyage seasonal and routine. Context only — no source ties it to sugar directly.
nodes.src: Periplus 57; Tchernia; Tripati (2011) via search summaries

nodes.label: Periplus §14
nodes.full: ‘Honey from the reed called sacchari’ is listed among goods carried from Ariaca and Barygaza to the ‘far-side’ African market-towns — the only trade record of cane honey in the period.

nodes.label: Dioscorides
nodes.full: Dioscorides describes a solidified honey called sakcharon found on reeds in India and Arabia Felix, like salt and brittle between the teeth, and prescribes it for the stomach, bladder and kidneys.
nodes.src: De materia medica 2.82, ed. Wellmann; Bouras-Vallianatos (2021) n.22

nodes.label: Galen
nodes.full: Galen adds to his entry on honey the ‘so-called sakchar’ from India and Arabia Felix: less sweet than honey, not bad for the stomach and not thirst-provoking — repeating report (‘as they say’), not experience.
nodes.src: De simpl. med. 7.9 (Kühn XII.71), Greek read in First1KGreek

nodes.label: Oribasius
nodes.full: Oribasius copies Galen’s remarks on sakchar into his Medical Collections; Alexander of Tralles, a clinician of wide pharmacological experience, never mentions the substance.

nodes.label: Nanyue 111 BC
nodes.full: After the Han conquer the southern kingdom of Nanyue, poets and officials reach the lands of the hundred Yue and begin to write about sugarcane.
nodes.src: Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.133 (Daniels); Needham SCC 6.3 p.141

nodes.label: Sima Xiangru
nodes.full: In the Zixu fu, Sima Xiangru lists zhuzhe, sugarcane, among the plants east of Yunmeng; a second poem has a court official using cane syrup to ease the effects of wine.

nodes.label: Zhao hun
nodes.full: The Chu ci poem offers stewed turtle and roast lamb with zhe jiang — cane syrup on most readings, yam sauce on Hawkes’s.

nodes.label: Southern Yue
nodes.full: Cane was part of the Yue diet before Han writers noticed it; the Han policy of sinicising the Yue met repeated rebellions. The people who grew the cane appear in the record as a frontier to be governed.

nodes.label: Shi mi
nodes.full: Before Indian methods arrived, the Chinese south made ‘stone honey’ by pressing cane and drying the juice in the sun; regular crystals needed the S. barberi and S. sinense hybrids.

nodes.label: Hou Hanshu
nodes.full: The Hou Hanshu’s treatise on India mentions shi mi among its products — cited by those who hold that at least some techniques for amorphous sugar came from India.

nodes.label: Yiwu zhi
nodes.full: Yang Fu’s Record of Strange Things: the best cane is Jiaozhi’s; boiled and sun-dried, the juice becomes shi mi, ‘stone honey’.
nodes.src: Needham SCC 6.3 p.143 n.d; Mazumdar (1998) p.18

nodes.label: Shuowen
nodes.full: Xu Shen’s dictionary gives the cane radical to every sugarcane name and equates zhe with zhuzhe.

nodes.label: Nanfang caomu
nodes.full: Ji Han’s botany describes Jiaozhi cane — sweet, a zhang tall — and the sun-dried juice some call shi mi, and records Funan’s tribute of cane in 285.

nodes.label: Funan 285
nodes.full: Funan presents sugarcane with three nodes to the zhang to the Western Jin court.

nodes.label: Jiaozhou syrup
nodes.full: Cane syrup sent as tribute from Jiaozhou sits in the Wu palace warehouse in the 250s, until a eunuch spoils it.

nodes.label: Liu Yiqing
nodes.full: Liu Yiqing describes Funan sugarcane as wilting in the sun and snapping in the wind — a southern curiosity at the southern courts.

nodes.label: Arthashastra
nodes.full: A list in the Arthaśāstra names five cane products in rising purity: phāṇita, guḍa, matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa, śarkarā.

nodes.label: Caraka, Suśruta
nodes.full: The Caraka and Suśruta saṃhitās distinguish cane clones and cane wine; the Bower manuscript (c.375) adds sugar candy, closing the ancient Indian inventory of sugars.

nodes.label: 3 boilings
nodes.full: A Buddhist sutra compares a monk’s progress to cane juice boiled once (phāṇita), twice (guḍa) and a third time until white (śarkarā; Chinese shimi).

nodes.label: Pali Vinaya
nodes.full: The Vinaya allows sick monks five tonics, among them molasses or syrup, even after midday.

nodes.label: Monastic rules
nodes.full: Chinese-translated codes: surplus cane is pressed and drunk in the evening, boiled to a syrup that keeps seven days, then heated to crystals that keep indefinitely.

nodes.label: Shapur I
nodes.full: Shapur I founds Gundeshapur, resettles captives at Susa and Tustar and — by Arabic tradition — has Roman prisoners build the Shushtar weir.

nodes.label: Deportees
nodes.full: Resettled captives and Valerian’s Roman prisoners remake Khuzestan: brocade weaving at Susa and Tustar, the weir at Shushtar.

nodes.label: Indian physician
nodes.full: Arabic sources say Shapur I brought a physician from India to teach medicine at Gundeshapur. No source ties this to sugar.
nodes.src: al-Tabari II p.845; al-Tha’alibi p.531 via Ouerfelli (2008) p.19 n.25

nodes.label: Armenian Geogr.
nodes.full: A text ascribed to Moses of Khorene puts sugar cane at Gundeshapur in Elymais and says sugar was ‘made artificially’ there.

nodes.label: Khusrau I
nodes.full: Under Khusrau I, Persian cane-growing is said to pass from gardens to the best lands of Khuzestan; the cane-juice anecdote about him is legend.

nodes.label: Sui shu
nodes.full: The Sui shu attributes shi mi (‘stone honey’) and ban mi (‘half honey’) to Persia and Cao — dated by what it describes, the late 6th century.

nodes.label: Word travels
nodes.full: Sanskrit śarkarā becomes Pali sakkharā and Greek sákchar, then Latin saccharum — the Indian word for granulated sugar reaches the Mediterranean as a medicine.

nodes.label: Sand sugar
nodes.full: Tao Hongjing notes shatang (‘sand sugar’) made at Guangzhou, and a Buddhist text translated in 488 confirms it; the name may echo śarkarā.

nodes.label: Mawangdui
nodes.full: Two bamboo slips of the Dai family tomb inventories are reported to carry the character for sugarcane (c.168 BC). Unverified lead.
nodes.src: Mazumdar (1998) p.17 — not checked against the excavation report

nodes.label: Xie Huilian
nodes.full: Xie Huilian’s requiem finds cane segments still joined in the water at the bottom of damaged coffins.

edges: The Greeks first met Indian cane juice on Alexander’s campaign; Theophrastus’s reed honey comes a generation later, though Ouerfelli finds his text unclear and it may mean bamboo manna.
Monsoon sailing made the voyages of the Indian Ocean routine; the Periplus is the merchant’s guide to that world, though its sacchari is cargo on the African leg, not the Egyptian one.

Ouerfelli, after Desanges: from before the middle of the 1st century AD knowledge of India grows through Red Sea commercial contacts, and the testimony on cane becomes more precise, notably in Dioscorides.
Galen’s remarks on sakchar were uncritically reproduced in Oribasius’s Medical Collections (Speculum n.23).

Daniels proposes that references to sugarcane begin to appear in Chinese literature in the 2nd century BC because of the Han conquests of the southern Yue; Sima Xiangru then names zhuzhe among the plants of Yunmeng.
The Han drive into the south brings the Yue under a policy of sinicisation (Needham), so the people who grew the cane enter the record as a frontier to be governed.
Daniels argues that the Han Chinese first learned the techniques for making amorphous sugar from the non-Han peoples of the south (Kieschnick n.138) — a view disputed by those who point to India.
Others stress Indian origins for some techniques, citing the Hou Hanshu’s mention of shi mi in India (Kieschnick n.139).
Needham notes that the Yiwu zhi passage of +90 closely resembles the wording of the Nanfang caomu zhuang; both describe Jiaozhi cane.
The Shuowen jiezi equated zhe and zhuzhe in 121; Ji Han’s botany then uses ‘zhuzhe, also called ganzhe’ — the same vocabulary line.
The commentary on Sima Xiangru’s zhuzhe (Zhang Yi) and Xu Shen’s dictionary equate the cane names — the vocabulary runs from the poet to the lexicographer.
Both are Chu-land poems: ‘Zhao hun’ names cane syrup c.241 BC and Sima Xiangru later sets zhuzhe among the plants of Yunmeng — Chu literature is where cane first appears.
Ji Han’s botany records Funan’s tribute of cane with three nodes to the zhang in 285.
Liu Yiqing’s Talk of the Times describes the same Funan cane in terms of its size, which Needham sets beside the tribute.
Mazumdar reads the Jiaozhou syrup tribute (Sanguozhi) and the Funan cane (Nanfang caomu zhuang) as one flow of cane products from Indochina to the Chinese courts.
The Arthaśāstra’s grades from guḍa to śarkarā reappear in the Caraka and Suśruta saṃhitās and in the Bower manuscript’s sugar candy, which Needham sets in sequence.
The ladder of grades known to the Indian medical texts is the same ladder the Buddhist sutra uses in its three boilings.
The Pali Vinaya’s permission for molasses as a monks’ tonic is the earliest layer of the cane rules that later codes, translated in 405–416, elaborate to syrup and crystals.
The monastic rules and the sutra share one picture — juice boiled to syrup, then to crystals — which Kieschnick reads as evidence of the Indian ladder.
Shapur I resettled captives at Susa and Tustar and, by Arabic tradition, set Valerian’s Roman prisoners to build the Shushtar weir.
Shapur I founded Gundeshapur and, according to al-Tabari and al-Tha’alibi, brought a physician from India to teach medicine there.
Ouerfelli asks whether Shapur’s works in Khuzestan relate to the introduction of cane there (‘peut-être possible’); the Armenian Geography later puts cane at Gundeshapur.
Cane is already grown near Gundeshapur by the 5th century; Ouerfelli sees its real development on the best Khuzestan lands from Khusrau I’s reign.
Persian cane develops in Khusrau I’s time, and the Sui shu then lists shi mi and ban mi among Persia’s products.
Sanskrit śarkarā may underlie the Chinese shatang (‘sand sugar’), made at Guangzhou by the late 5th century (Mazumdar; Kieschnick).
Cane as a funerary offering recurs: the Mawangdui inventory (168 BC) and the Jiangsu coffins of Xie Huilian’s requiem (c.400).
